## Proof

**Answer: Yes.** The boundedness of $T: H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^n) \to H^s(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for all $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$ implies that $T$ is continuous from $H^{-\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to $H^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

### Setup: the two limit topologies

**$H^\infty$ as a projective limit.** We have
$$H^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n) = \bigcap_{s \in \mathbb{N}} H^s(\mathbb{R}^n) = \underset{s}{\text{proj}}\, H^s(\mathbb{R}^n),$$
equipped with the Fréchet topology generated by the seminorms $p_s(u) = \|u\|_{H^s}$. The inclusions $H^{s+1} \hookrightarrow H^s$ are compact (by the Rellich–Kondrachov theorem for Sobolev spaces on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using the compactness of the embedding on bounded domains and the decay properties of the Fourier characterization), so $H^\infty$ is a **Fréchet–Schwartz space**.

**$H^{-\infty}$ as an inductive limit.** We have
$$H^{-\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n) = (H^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n))' = \bigcup_{r \in \mathbb{N}} H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \underset{r}{\text{ind}}\, H^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^n),$$
equipped with the locally convex inductive limit topology (which, since $H^\infty$ is Fréchet–Schwartz, coincides with the strong dual topology, making $H^{-\infty}$ a **DFS space / Silva space**). The inclusions $H^{-r} \hookrightarrow H^{-(r+1)}$ are continuous with dense image.

### Key characterization of continuous seminorms on the inductive limit

**Lemma.** A seminorm $p$ on $H^{-\infty} = \text{ind}_r\, H^{-r}$ is continuous if and only if $p\big|_{H^{-r}}$ is continuous on $H^{-r}$ for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$.

*Proof of Lemma.* This is a standard property of locally convex inductive limits. The inductive limit topology is the **finest** locally convex topology on $H^{-\infty}$ making all inclusions $\iota_r: H^{-r} \hookrightarrow H^{-\infty}$ continuous. A seminorm $p$ on a locally convex space is continuous if and only if it is dominated by a finite sum of the defining seminorms. By the universal property of the inductive limit, $p$ is continuous on $H^{-\infty}$ if and only if $p \circ \iota_r$ is continuous on $H^{-r}$ for each $r$, i.e., $p\big|_{H^{-r}}$ is continuous for each $r$. $\square$

### Key characterization of continuous maps into the projective limit

**Lemma.** A linear map $T: H^{-\infty} \to H^\infty = \text{proj}_s\, H^s$ is continuous if and only if for every $s \in \mathbb{N}$, the seminorm $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ is continuous on $H^{-\infty}$.

*Proof of Lemma.* The projective limit topology on $H^\infty$ is the coarsest topology making all projections $\pi_s: H^\infty \to H^s$ continuous. A linear map into a projective limit is continuous if and only if its composition with each projection is continuous. Here $\pi_s \circ T: H^{-\infty} \to H^s$ is continuous if and only if $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ is a continuous seminorm on $H^{-\infty}$. $\square$

### Combining the two characterizations

$T: H^{-\infty} \to H^\infty$ is continuous
$\iff$ for every $s \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ is a continuous seminorm on $H^{-\infty}$ (by the second Lemma)
$\iff$ for every $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ is continuous on $H^{-r}$ (by the first Lemma)
$\iff$ for every $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$, $T\big|_{H^{-r}}: H^{-r} \to H^s$ is a bounded operator.

The last equivalence holds because a linear map between Hilbert spaces is bounded if and only if it is continuous, and continuity of $T\big|_{H^{-r}}: H^{-r} \to H^s$ is equivalent to continuity of the seminorm $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ on $H^{-r}$.

### Conclusion

The hypothesis states exactly that $T\big|_{H^{-r}}: H^{-r} \to H^s$ is bounded for all $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$. By the chain of equivalences above, this is equivalent to $T: H^{-\infty} \to H^\infty$ being continuous. Therefore:

**Yes, the boundedness of $T$ from $H^{-r}$ to $H^s$ for all $r, s \in \mathbb{N}$ implies that $T$ defines a continuous operator from $H^{-\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to $H^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$.**

### Remark on the inequality

The given inequality $\|T\varphi\|_{H^s} \le M_s \cdot \max_{1 \le j \le N_s} |\varphi(f_j)|$ with $f_j \in H^\infty$ provides an *explicit* continuity estimate: each map $\varphi \mapsto \varphi(f_j) = \langle \varphi, f_j \rangle$ is a continuous linear functional on $H^{-\infty} = (H^\infty)'$ (since $f_j \in H^\infty$), so $\max_j |\varphi(f_j)|$ is a continuous seminorm on $H^{-\infty}$, and the inequality directly exhibits $\varphi \mapsto \|T\varphi\|_{H^s}$ as a continuous seminorm. This is consistent with — and in fact stronger than — what the componentwise boundedness gives us, since it shows the continuity factors through a finite-dimensional quotient of $H^{-\infty}$. The componentwise boundedness condition alone, however, is already sufficient by the inductive/projective limit argument above.
